opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me, Peter. It's a great question, and the honest answer is: we know a lot less than people think, and a lot more than we did twenty years ago.

I like to put it this way. If you imagine everything there is to know about the brain as a big book, we've maybe read the table of contents and a few chapters. We know the general layout. We know that certain regions are involved in vision, in language, in memory, in movement. We know a lot about how a single neuron works: how it fires, how it communicates chemically and electrically with its neighbors. That's the micro level, and it's pretty well understood.

We also know quite a bit at the macro level, from imaging and from patients with injuries. If someone damages a certain area, they lose the ability to recognize faces, or to form new memories. So we can map functions onto regions.

What we really don't understand is the middle: how roughly 86 billion neurons, each with thousands of connections, come together to produce a thought, a decision, a sense of self. How does electrical activity become the experience of tasting coffee or falling in love? That's the big gap, and frankly we don't even fully have the right language or tools for it yet.

My own work involves recording from individual neurons in patients who are undergoing brain surgery, so I get a very intimate view. I can sometimes see a single cell respond when someone thinks of a specific person or concept. That's thrilling, but it's also humbling, because you realize you're listening to one voice in a stadium of billions and trying to infer what the whole crowd is chanting.

So I'd say we're in an early but exciting phase. Something like physics before Newton: we have lots of observations, some good local theories, but no unifying framework. The tools are improving very fast, and with AI and better recording technology I think the next couple of decades will be remarkable. But anyone who tells you we've figured out the brain is overselling it.

r001.rationale: It says neuron firing and communication are fairly well understood, while how neural activity produces thought and experience remains a major gap.

r002.rationale: It describes recent progress and future advances, but does not characterize the history as long periods of little progress punctuated by major leaps.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'd say we understand very little, and I say that as someone who has spent most of my adult life looking at the brain. If you asked me to put a number on it, and people always want a number, I'd say we're maybe at five percent, and I'm probably being generous.

Here's the way I think about it. We have gotten extremely good at the level of the single neuron. We know how a cell fires, how it communicates with its neighbors, what chemicals are involved. We know that beautifully. And we've gotten reasonably good at the very large scale, where you put someone in an fMRI scanner and you can say, okay, this region lights up when they see a face, this region is involved in fear. But the thing in the middle, how 86 billion of these cells coordinate to produce a thought, a memory, a decision, the feeling of being you, that's where we're basically in the dark. It's like understanding every transistor in a computer, and being able to see that the screen gets warm when it runs a game, and having no idea what software is.

And the humbling part is that every decade we think we've cracked it. In the sixties it was the computer metaphor. Then it was neural networks. Now it's AI and large language models, and everyone says, ah, the brain is probably like that. And every time, the brain turns out to be weirder than the metaphor.

What I'd add, and I think this is what makes it interesting rather than depressing, is that the questions we can ask now are completely different from the ones we could ask twenty years ago. I work with patients who have electrodes implanted directly in their brains, usually for epilepsy, and we can listen to individual neurons while a person is making a choice, or dreaming, or recalling a memory. We can sometimes predict what someone will decide before they tell us they've decided. That's genuinely new. So we don't understand the brain, but we're finally in a position to be confused at a much higher level than before. And in science, being confused at a higher level is what progress looks like.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts detailed knowledge of individual neurons, signaling, and brain regions with limited understanding of how those parts coordinate to produce thought, memory, and decisions.

r002.rationale: It describes changing metaphors and newer research capabilities, but does not characterize progress as long periods of little progress punctuated by major leaps.

astra-6.text:
I think we understand a lot about certain pieces, and much less about how those pieces come together. We can study an individual neuron and describe how it sends a signal. We can identify networks involved in vision, memory, or movement. But going from that to explaining how you experience a memory, or why you make a particular decision, is a much bigger leap.

So I’m hesitant to put a percentage on it. To say we understand ten percent would imply that we know what the whole hundred percent looks like. We don’t.

And there’s a difference between predicting something and understanding it. If I can look at your brain activity and predict what you’re about to do, that’s useful. But it doesn’t necessarily mean I can explain the entire process that produced your choice. We’ve made real progress, but those different levels of explanation still don’t fit together completely.

r001.rationale: It contrasts describing neuron signals and identifying brain networks with explaining experiences and decisions, distinguishing knowledge of brain components from understanding how they work together.

r002.rationale: It says progress has been real but that levels of explanation do not fully fit together; it does not describe progress as long periods of little change punctuated by major leaps.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we understand a lot of pieces, but we don’t yet understand how those pieces come together. We know quite a bit about how an individual neuron works. We can measure activity in different parts of the brain and connect that activity to things like seeing, moving, or remembering. But going from those measurements to explaining your experience—why something feels a certain way, how a memory becomes part of who you are—that’s still a huge challenge.

And there’s a funny thing in neuroscience: the more we discover, the more precise our questions become, and the more we realize we have left to explain. So I wouldn’t give you a percentage. We don’t know the size of the thing we’re trying to understand well enough to say we’ve understood ten percent of it.

We’ve made real progress. But predicting what an entire human brain will do, or explaining how its activity gives rise to a mind? We’re still a long way from that.

r001.rationale: It contrasts what we know about individual neurons and measured brain activity linked to specific functions with our lack of understanding of how those pieces combine into a mind.

r002.rationale: It describes progress and remaining challenges, but does not characterize progress as long periods of little change punctuated by major leaps.
